newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk CB policy aims to brake inflation at 80 pct.
newsitem.headline: Turk CB policy aims to brake inflation at 80 pct.

text.p: Turkish Central Bank Governor Gazi Ercel said on Wednesday the bank would continue to implement monetary policies to prevent 1996 inflation from rising over his forecast of 80 percent.

"I would like to stress that the Central Bank will take pains with limits and developments on monetary indicators and continue to implement a monetary policy which will not cause any further rise in inflation which we forecast at 80 percent for this year," Ercel said in written remarks prepared for Reuters.
Ercel's remarks did not clarify whether he meant wholesale or consumer price inflation.
Turkey's year-on-year inflation was 81.2 percent in consumer prices and 76.3 percent in wholesale prices in July.

"It is estimated that the budget will give a surplus of two percent of GNP (Gross National Product) excluding interest in 1996," he said. Last year the ratio of primary surplus to GNP was 3.4 percent.
Ercel said the bank's ultimate target of lowering inflation to single digits could only be achieved by implementing a credible medium-term programme.
"The ultimate goal of the Central Bank is to reduce inflation to a single digit and keep it there. This is doubtlessly not a matter that the Central Bank can realise alone," he said.
"Macro-economic policies should be drawn up in an anti-inflationary way which can be achieved through a credible medium-term programme that targets to lower inflation," he said.
Ercel said the central bank's monetary programme aimed at curbing inflation by restraining growth in money supply -- M1 and M2 -- through controlling reserve money.
"The low level of annual rise in reserve money at a period when inflation runs at 70-80 percent and real interest rates at 25-30 percent shows how realistic the monetary policy is," he said.
The annualised rise in the reserve money was 64.3 percent in July and 69 percent on August 23, he said.
"The implementation of the monetary policy requires fine tuning," said Ercel.

He said the central bank had used open market operations and foreign currency transactions to smooth "significant fluctuations" in monetary indicators caused by the government's higher-than-expected civil servant pay rises and treasury's reliance on the central bank funds for payments worth 75 trillion lira in July.
He said relations between the central bank and treasury have been constructive.
